pos: n. (the Cistercian convent near Celle, founded c. 1230, Lutheran since the Reformation and still a women's foundation)
etymology: From Middle Low German, the houses by the pasture; Haus, a house.
biblical_def: Wienhausen near Celle in Lower Saxony was founded about 1230 for Cistercian nuns and is the best preserved of the Lüneburg convents. Its nuns' choir, painted from floor to vault about 1335, is almost intact, and the house keeps a set of large medieval tapestries worked by the sisters themselves. In 1953 a cache of small objects lost through the floorboards was recovered, including spectacles, bobbins, pins and the oldest surviving pair of eyeglasses in Europe. The convent accepted the Reformation in 1587 and has continued without interruption to this day as a Lutheran women's foundation. This dictionary records Wienhausen for the work of its women's hands, which Scripture praises directly and in detail. The capable woman is described at her loom, “She seeketh wool, and flax, and worketh willingly with her hands” (Pro 31:13), and her tapestry is named, “She maketh herself coverings of tapestry” (Pro 31:22). The skilled women who furnished the tabernacle are commended by name, “And all the women that were wise hearted did spin with their hands” (Exo 35:25), and the teaching of the younger by the older is a standing charge, “teachers of good things” (Tit 2:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a convent as a body of monks or nuns; tapestry as a kind of woven hangings; to spin as to draw out and twist into threads; needlework as work done with a needle; and a distaff as the staff from which flax is drawn.
webster_full: CONVENT, n. An assembly of persons devoted to religion; a body of monks or nuns; also, the house occupied by such a society.
TAPESTRY, n. A kind of woven hangings of wool and silk, often enriched with gold and silver, representing figures of men, animals, landscapes.
SPIN, v.t. To draw out and twist into threads, either by the hand or by machinery; as, to spin wool, cotton or flax.
NEEDLEWORK, n. Work executed with a needle; the business of a seamstress; embroidery by the needle.
DISTAFF, n. The staff of a spinning wheel, to which a bunch of flax or tow is tied, and from which the thread is drawn.
scriptures: She seeketh wool, and flax, and worketh willingly with her hands.
She maketh herself coverings of tapestry; her clothing is silk and purple.
And all the women that were wise hearted did spin with their hands, and brought that which they had spun, both of blue, and of purple, and of scarlet, and of fine linen.
The aged women likewise, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things;
corruption_summary: Cistercian convent near Celle, c. 1230: a painted nuns' choir, tapestries worked by the sisters, and an unbroken life through the Reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture praises women's skilled work concretely rather than abstractly. Proverbs puts a woman at her wool and flax and calls the willingness itself a virtue, “and worketh willingly with her hands” (Pro 31:13), then names the product, “She maketh herself coverings of tapestry” (Pro 31:22). Exodus records the spinners of the tabernacle as wise hearted, which is the same phrase used of Bezaleel, “And all the women that were wise hearted did spin with their hands” (Exo 35:25).

The second thing is the continuity. Wienhausen did not have to be destroyed to be reformed; it accepted evangelical preaching in 1587 and has been a Lutheran women's foundation ever since, which is nearly four centuries longer than its Catholic life. The pattern Paul gives for such a household is older women teaching younger ones in the ordinary business of living, “The aged women likewise, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness” (Tit 2:3), “That they may teach the young women to be sober” (Tit 2:4).

Greek kalodidaskalos (G2567) — a teacher of what is good; “teachers of good things”, Titus 2:3.

“that were wise hearted did spin with their hands” (Exo 35:25) — the same word used of the tabernacle's chief craftsman.
“That they may teach the young women to be sober” (Tit 2:4) — the charge a women's house exists to keep.

pos: n. (one of the six Lüneburg convents, Cistercian from 1243, Lutheran since 1540)
etymology: From Middle Low German isen, iron, and hagen, an enclosure; the iron hedge.
biblical_def: Isenhagen, near Hankensbüttel in Lower Saxony, was founded in 1243 by Duke Otto the Child, first as a double house and then as a Cistercian convent of women. It is one of the six Lüneburg Heideklöster, with Wienhausen, Medingen, Ebstorf, Lüne and Walsrode, all of which accepted the Reformation under Duke Ernest the Confessor and all of which still exist as Protestant women's foundations administered by a common chamber. Isenhagen keeps a late Gothic winged altar and a notable collection of textiles. This dictionary records the house and its five sisters for the fact that most readers find surprising: the Reformation did not everywhere dissolve. Where a community would hear the word, it was taught rather than evicted, which is what Scripture would expect of a reform, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine” (2Ti 3:16). The company that carries the word is not reckoned small, “great was the company of those that published it” (Psa 68:11). Faith is handed down through women in Paul's own example, “which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois” (2Ti 1:5), and the ornament commended is interior, “the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit” (1Pe 3:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a foundation as an endowment; a chapter as an assembly of ecclesiastics; reformation as a change from worse to better; an abbess as the governess of a nunnery; and endowment as the settling of a fund upon an institution.
webster_full: FOUNDATION, n. The basis or groundwork of any thing; also, endowment; a donation or legacy appropriated to support an institution.
CHAPTER, n. An assembly of the clergy of a cathedral or collegiate church, or of the members of a religious order.
REFORMATION, n. Change from worse to better; amendment of life; in history, the change of religion from the corruptions of popery to its primitive purity.
ABBESS, n. The governess of a nunnery or convent of nuns, having the same rank and authority over the nuns that the abbots have over the monks.
ENDOWMENT, n. The act of settling a fund or permanent provision for the support of an institution; the fund so settled.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it.
When I call to remembrance the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice; and I am persuaded that in thee also.
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
corruption_summary: One of six Lüneburg convents, Cistercian from 1243: taught rather than dissolved at the Reformation, and still a women's foundation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that reform at its best replaces bad teaching with good rather than simply seizing buildings. The six Lüneburg houses were preached to, argued with, and in several cases resisted hard before they yielded; they were not emptied. Scripture gives the instrument and the warrant, “profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness” (2Ti 3:16).

The second thing is the standing of the women who stayed. Paul traces Timothy's faith back through two generations of women without embarrassment, “which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice” (2Ti 1:5), and Peter locates a woman's true adornment where no habit and no jewellery can reach, “even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price” (1Pe 3:4). A Protestant foundation of unmarried women is an odd survival, and it has outlasted a great many arrangements that looked sturdier.

“which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois” (2Ti 1:5) — faith handed down through women.
“the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit” (1Pe 3:4) — what no habit supplies and none prevents.

pos: n. (the Lüneburg Cistercian convent of 1228, rebuilt in classical style after the fire of 1781)
etymology: From a Low German place name in -ingen, the settlement of Mado's people.
biblical_def: Medingen near Bad Bevensen in Lower Saxony was founded in 1228 and moved to its present site in 1336. It is another of the six Lüneburg convents that passed into Protestant hands in the sixteenth century, and it is the one whose medieval fabric did not survive: a fire in 1781 destroyed the buildings, which were rebuilt in a restrained classical style, so that Medingen is now a white neoclassical cloister with a Protestant abbess and conventuals. Its late medieval prayer books, written and illuminated by the nuns in a mixture of Latin and Low German, survive in libraries across Europe. This dictionary records Medingen for those books, because a house of women writing their own devotional manuscripts is a thing worth noticing. Scripture puts the word on the tongue of the household, “And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children” (Deu 6:7), and the writing of it is commanded outright, “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables” (Hab 2:2). Meditation on the law is the psalmist's whole occupation, “in his law doth he meditate day and night” (Psa 1:2), and the fire that took the buildings took nothing that mattered most, “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a breviary as a book containing the daily service; a manuscript as a book written by hand; to illuminate as to adorn with pictures; devotion as the performance of religious duties; and a vernacular as the native language of a country.
webster_full: BREVIARY, n. A book containing the daily service of the Romish church; an abridgment; a compend; an epitome.
MANUSCRIPT, n. A book or paper written with the hand or pen; a writing of any kind, in distinction from what is printed.
ILLUMINATE, v.t. To adorn with pictures or portraits, as manuscripts; to enlighten intellectually; to supply with light.
DEVOTION, n. The state of being dedicated or consecrated; piety; the performance of religious duties; prayer.
VERNACULAR, adj. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as, the vernacular tongue or idiom.
scriptures: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
corruption_summary: Lüneburg convent of 1228, rebuilt in white classical stone after the fire of 1781: its nuns' own prayer books outlived its walls.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that devotional writing in a person's own language is an old practice, not a modern one. The Medingen sisters wrote prayer books that moved between Latin and the Low German they actually spoke, which is the instinct behind the command to put the word where it can be read at speed, “make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2), and behind the household teaching Moses prescribes, “and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house” (Deu 6:7).

The second thing is the fire. Medingen lost everything built and kept everything written, which is a parable about what endures. The psalmist's occupation needs no building, “But his delight is in the law of the LORD” (Psa 1:2), and Isaiah states the contrast between what fades and what does not without qualification, “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8). A convent with a new roof and its old books lost less than it looked.

Hebrew nabel (H5034) — to wither, to fade away; “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth”, Isaiah 40:8.

“in his law doth he meditate day and night” (Psa 1:2) — an occupation a fire cannot reach.
“but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) — what Medingen kept when the buildings went.

pos: n. (the Lüneburg convent, home of the Ebstorf Map, the largest known medieval world map)
etymology: From Middle Low German, the village on the river Eb; dorf, a village.
biblical_def: Ebstorf on the Lüneburg Heath was a Premonstratensian and then Benedictine house of women, rebuilt after 1197, and is another of the six convents that became Protestant foundations in the sixteenth century. Its fame rests on a single object. The Ebstorf Map, made about 1300, was the largest known medieval mappa mundi, some three and a half metres across, drawn on thirty goatskins. It was rediscovered in the convent in 1830 and destroyed by bombing in Hanover in 1943; only photographs and copies remain. The map places Jerusalem at the centre and sets Christ's head at the top, his hands at the sides and his feet at the bottom, so that the whole world is held inside his body. This dictionary records Ebstorf for that image, because it is a theological claim before it is a geographical one, and the claim is biblical. The world belongs to God outright, “The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof” (Psa 24:1). All things hold together in Christ, “he is before all things, and by him all things consist” (Col 1:17). Existence itself is located in him, “For in him we live, and move, and have our being” (Act 17:28), and the whole runs from him and back, “For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things” (Rom 11:36).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a map as a representation of the earth's surface; the world as the whole system of created things; geography as the science of the earth's surface; the universe as the whole system of created things; and creation as the act of causing to exist.
webster_full: MAP, n. A representation of the surface of the earth, or of any part of it, drawn on paper or other material, exhibiting the lines of latitude and longitude.
WORLD, n. The universe; the whole system of created things; also, the earth; the terraqueous globe; also, present state of existence.
GEOGRAPHY, n. The science or knowledge of the earth, and of its inhabitants, and of the various natural divisions of its surface.
UNIVERSE, n. The collective name of heaven and earth, and all that belongs to them; the whole system of created things.
CREATION, n. The act of creating; the act of causing to exist; and especially, the act of bringing this world into existence.
scriptures: A Psalm of David. The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein.
And he is before all things, and by him all things consist.
For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.
For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen.
corruption_summary: Lüneburg convent and home of the Ebstorf Map, c. 1300: a world drawn inside the body of Christ, lost to bombing in 1943.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the map's own claim. Setting Christ's head, hands and feet at the four edges of the world was not a decorative conceit; it asserts that the creation is held within his dominion, which is what the psalm says without a picture, “The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein” (Psa 24:1), and what Paul says in a sentence the map could have been drawn from, “by him all things consist” (Col 1:17).

The second thing Ebstorf illustrates is how a frame determines what a map is for. A modern map answers where things are; the Ebstorf map answers whose they are, and it is wrong about distances and right about ownership. Paul grants a pagan poet a true sentence and keeps it, “For in him we live, and move, and have our being” (Act 17:28), then draws the whole circuit closed, “For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever” (Rom 11:36). A goatskin world lost in an air raid still said something true.

“by him all things consist” (Col 1:17) — the sentence the goatskins were drawn from.

pos: n. (the Cistercian convent near Lüneburg, moved to its site in 1243 and dissolved at the Reformation)
etymology: From Middle Low German scharn, dung or a shambles, and beck, a brook.
biblical_def: Scharnebeck, east of Lüneburg, was founded in 1243 when a community of Cistercian women was moved to the site from an earlier location, and it held lands and a mill on the Ilmenau. Unlike its five better-known sisters on the heath it did not survive the Reformation as a foundation; it was dissolved in the sixteenth century and its buildings largely taken down, and the village today is better known for the twentieth-century ship lift that raises barges forty-eight metres between two canals. This dictionary records Scharnebeck for the contrast with its neighbours, and for what the name itself offers: a brook running past a place where refuse was thrown. Scripture is not squeamish about such places, and its most important event happened outside the gate where the refuse went, “Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered without the gate” (Heb 13:12). Believers are told to go out to him there, “Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb 13:13). Paul takes the same word for refuse to himself, “I count all things but loss” (Phi 3:8), and the discarded stone is the one that holds, “The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner” (Psa 118:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines refuse as that which is rejected as worthless; a brook as a small stream; to dissolve as to break up or put an end to; reproach as censure or infamy; and a cornerstone as the stone which lies at the corner of a building.
webster_full: REFUSE, n. That which is refused or rejected as useless; waste matter; dross; dregs; recrement.
BROOK, n. A small natural stream of water, or a current flowing from a spring or fountain, less than a river.
DISSOLVE, v.t. To break up, applied to assemblies; to separate a body into its component parts; to put an end to.
REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt or derision; contumelious or opprobrious language; also, infamy; shame.
CORNERSTONE, n. The stone which lies at the corner of two walls, and unites them; the principal stone, and especially the stone which forms the corner of the foundation.
scriptures: Wherefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered without the gate.
Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach.

Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,
The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.
corruption_summary: Cistercian convent near Lüneburg, 1243: the one heath house that did not survive the Reformation, and whose name means the brook by the refuse.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture locates the decisive events at the rubbish end of town. The crucifixion happened outside the gate where the refuse and the carcases went, and Hebrews makes the location part of the argument, “suffered without the gate” (Heb 13:12). The instruction follows immediately and is uncomfortable, “Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb 13:13).

The second thing is the pattern of what is thrown out and then turns out to be essential. Paul uses the strongest available word for refuse about his own best credentials, “I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord” (Phi 3:8), and the psalm the apostles quoted most often is about a stone the professionals discarded, “The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner” (Psa 118:22). A convent whose name means the dung brook, dissolved and forgotten beside its famous sisters, is not a bad place to be reminded of it.

pos: n. (the Cistercian abbey near Fribourg, founded 1138, still a living community)
etymology: French haute rive, the high bank, of the Sarine; Latin Altaripa.
biblical_def: Hauterive stands on a bend of the Sarine south of Fribourg and was founded in 1138 by Guillaume de Glâne, settled from Cherlieu. Its church, consecrated in 1160, keeps its Cistercian plan; the cloister was rebuilt in the fourteenth century and holds some of the best Gothic glass in Switzerland. The house was suppressed by the canton in 1848 and the buildings used as a teachers' college, but monks returned in 1939 and Hauterive is a working abbey today, one of the few medieval Swiss houses with an unbroken community again in its own cloister. This dictionary records Hauterive for the return, which is a biblical motion rather than a sentimental one. Scripture treats the rebuilding of what was thrown down as God's own promise, “they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations” (Isa 61:4), and Nehemiah makes it a work to be organised rather than merely desired, “come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem” (Neh 2:17). The affection that drives it is for the stones themselves, “For thy servants take pleasure in her stones, and favour the dust thereof” (Psa 102:14), and the building that matters is never the masonry, “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psa 127:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to restore as to bring back to a former state; a ruin as the remains of a decayed building; to rebuild as to build again; desolation as a place laid waste; and perseverance as persistence in a course begun.
webster_full: RESTORE, v.t. To return to a person, as a specific thing which he has lost; to bring back; to heal; to bring back to a former state.
RUIN, n. Destruction; fall; overthrow; also, in the plural, the remains of a decayed or demolished city, house or other work of men.
REBUILD, v.t. To build again; to repair or restore any thing that has been demolished or thrown down.
DESOLATION, n. The act of desolating; destruction of inhabitants; a place deprived of inhabitants or otherwise wasted.
PERSEVERANCE, n. Persistence in any business or enterprise undertaken; continuance in a state of grace to the end.
scriptures: And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations.

Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.
For thy servants take pleasure in her stones, and favour the dust thereof.
A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
corruption_summary: Swiss Cistercian abbey of 1138: suppressed in 1848, a teachers' college for ninety years, and a living community again since 1939.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that restoration is a work God names and claims. Isaiah does not promise that the ruins will be admired; he promises that they will be built, with generations of desolation reversed, “they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations” (Isa 61:4). Nehemiah's contribution is to say it out loud to people who had grown used to rubble, “Ye see the distress that we are in” (Neh 2:17).

The second thing is the affection that makes restoration possible. The psalm does not say the servants pleaded the strategic importance of Zion; it says they loved its broken stones and even its dust, “and favour the dust thereof” (Psa 102:14). That is what brought monks back to Hauterive in 1939 after ninety years. The caution is in the next psalm quoted, which refuses to let the builders congratulate themselves, “except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Psa 127:1).

Hebrew banah (H1129) — to build, to rebuild a wall; “let us build up the wall of Jerusalem”, Nehemiah 2:17.
Hebrew ratsah (H7521) — to be pleased with, to delight in; “thy servants take pleasure in her stones”, Psalm 102:14.
Hebrew 'aphar (H6083) — dust, loved for the place's sake; “and favour the dust thereof”, Psalm 102:14.
Hebrew shaw' (H7723) — emptiness, labour to no purpose; “they labour in vain that build it”, Psalm 127:1.
usage: “they shall build the old wastes” (Isa 61:4) — restoration promised, not merely hoped.
“thy servants take pleasure in her stones” (Psa 102:14) — the affection that brings people back.
“Except the LORD build the house” (Psa 127:1) — the clause that keeps a restoration humble.

pos: n. (the Cistercian abbey above Nyon in the Vaud, founded 1131, its church now standing in a golf course)
etymology: French bon mont, the good hill; Latin Bonus Mons.
biblical_def: Bonmont above Nyon in the canton of Vaud was founded as a house of canons about 1123 and affiliated to Cîteaux in 1131 through Clairvaux, the first Cistercian house in what is now French-speaking Switzerland. It was secularised at the Bernese Reformation in 1536, the lands passed through several families, and the twelfth-century church, a plain Romanesque basilica of great severity, was used for centuries as a barn and a cellar. The estate is now a golf club, and the restored church stands in the middle of the course and is used for concerts. This dictionary records Bonmont because that ending puts a question many Protestants answer too quickly. If a building is not holy, is nothing lost when it becomes a clubhouse? Scripture says the Most High does not live in buildings, “dwelleth not in temples made with hands” (Act 17:24), and Solomon said it first at the dedication of the only temple God ever commanded, “the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee” (1Ki 8:27). Yet the Lord was fierce about the use of a house called by his name, “My house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer” (Mar 11:17), “make not my Father's house an house of merchandise” (Joh 2:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to secularise as to convert from sacred to common use; profane as unholy or irreverent; a temple as a building for worship; consecration as the act of devoting to sacred use; and desecration as the act of diverting from a sacred purpose.
webster_full: SECULARIZE, v.t. To convert from spiritual or ecclesiastical appropriation to secular or common use.
PROFANE, adj. Not sacred; secular; irreverent to any thing sacred; polluted; not pure.
TEMPLE, n. A public edifice erected in honor of some deity; among Christians, a church; a place appropriated to the worship of God.
CONSECRATION, n. The act or ceremony of separating from a common to a sacred use, or of devoting and dedicating a person or thing to the service of God.
DESECRATE, v.t. To divert from a sacred purpose or appropriation; to convert from a sacred to a profane use.
scriptures: God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands;
But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?
And he taught, saying unto them, Is it not written, My house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer? but ye have made it a den of thieves.
And said unto them that sold doves, Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise.
corruption_summary: Vaudois abbey of 1131: a severe Romanesque church used as a barn for centuries and now standing on a golf course.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is both halves of Scripture's answer, which most people hold only one of. God is not housed, and Paul says so to a city full of temples, “dwelleth not in temples made with hands” (Act 17:24); Solomon had conceded the same point while dedicating the temple itself, “But will God indeed dwell on the earth?” (1Ki 8:27). So a church building is not a sacrament, and a Protestant is right to say so.

The other half is that the Lord cared intensely about what a house bearing his name was used for, and acted about it, “Is it not written, My house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer?” (Mar 11:17), “Take these things hence” (Joh 2:16). The objection there was commerce inside a place of prayer, which is a sharper question for a church that keeps its building and fills it with trade than for one that lost its building to a golf club. The principle to recover is that the use, not the masonry, is what God watches.
roots_summary: Greek naos (G3485), a temple; Greek cheiropoietos (G5499), made with hands; Hebrew kul (H3557), to contain; Greek proseuche (G4335), prayer; Greek emporion (G1712), a place of merchandise.
roots_lines: Greek cheiropoietos (G5499) — made with hands, of temples; “dwelleth not in temples made with hands”, Acts 17:24.
Hebrew kul (H3557) — to hold, to contain; “the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee”, 1 Kings 8:27.
Greek proseuche (G4335) — prayer, the house's purpose; “My house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer”, Mark 11:17.
Greek emporion (G1712) — a market, a place of trade; “make not my Father's house an house of merchandise”, John 2:16.
Greek lestes (G3027) — a robber, what the house had become; “but ye have made it a den of thieves”, Mark 11:17.
usage: “dwelleth not in temples made with hands” (Act 17:24) — the half most Protestants remember.
“make not my Father's house an house of merchandise” (Joh 2:16) — the half they often forget.
“But will God indeed dwell on the earth?” (1Ki 8:27) — conceded by the man dedicating the temple.

pos: n. (the Bernese Cistercian abbey of 1131, dissolved in 1528 and turned to the care of the poor)
etymology: From a Germanic personal name with Berg, a hill; Latin Aurora, the dawn.
biblical_def: Frienisberg north of Bern was founded in 1131 from Lucelle and was known in Latin as Aurora, the dawn. It was one of the wealthiest houses in the Bernese lands, holding granges, vineyards and tithes across the Seeland. At the Bernese Reformation in 1528 the city secularised it, and rather than selling the estate outright the council eventually turned the buildings to the relief of the poor; Frienisberg served as a poorhouse, then a workhouse and then an institution for the aged, and it still functions as a home for the elderly. This dictionary records Frienisberg because that reuse is the best answer a Reformation ever gave to the question of what to do with a dissolved abbey. Scripture ties fasting and true religion to feeding and housing, “Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house?” (Isa 58:7). Christ puts the sick and the imprisoned in the place of himself, “I was sick, and ye visited me” (Mat 25:36). Words without provision are condemned outright, “Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful” (Jam 2:16), and the poor man's creditor is God, “He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD” (Pro 19:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an almshouse as a house for the poor; charity as liberality to the poor; the poor as those destitute of property; relief as the removal of pain or want; and a hospital as a building for the sick or needy.
webster_full: ALMSHOUSE, n. A house appropriated for the use of the poor, who are supported by the public, or by charity.
CHARITY, n. Liberality to the poor, consisting in almsgiving or benefactions, or in gratuitous services to relieve them in distress.
POOR, adj. Wholly destitute of property, or not having property sufficient for a comfortable subsistence; needy.
RELIEF, n. The removal, in whole or in part, of any evil that afflicts the body or mind; alleviation of pain or distress.
HOSPITAL, n. A building appropriated for the reception of sick, infirm and helpless paupers, who are supported and nursed by charity.
scriptures: Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?
Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.
And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?
He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD; and that which he hath given will he pay him again.
corruption_summary: Bernese abbey of 1131 called the dawn: secularised in 1528 and given to the care of the poor, which it still is.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a reformation is judged partly by what it does with what it takes. Bern seized a rich abbey and eventually put it to feeding and housing the destitute, which is exactly where Isaiah locates the fast God chooses, “Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry” (Isa 58:7), and where Christ locates himself, “I was sick, and ye visited me” (Mat 25:36).

The live corruption is the substitution of sentiment for supply, which James attacks in one of the most unanswerable sentences in the New Testament, “be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body” (Jam 2:16). Proverbs supplies the motive that keeps such work from condescension by naming who the actual creditor is, “He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD; and that which he hath given will he pay him again” (Pro 19:17). A house called the dawn that became a poorhouse improved its name.
roots_summary: Hebrew lechem (H3899), bread; Greek episkeptomai (G1980), to visit; Greek epitedeios (G2006), needful; Hebrew chanan (H2603), to show pity; Hebrew dal (H1800), the poor.
roots_lines: Hebrew lechem (H3899) — bread, to be broken out to others; “Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry”, Isaiah 58:7.
Hebrew marud (H4788) — the cast out, the homeless poor; “that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house”, Isaiah 58:7.
Greek episkeptomai (G1980) — to look in upon, to visit; “I was sick, and ye visited me”, Matthew 25:36.
Greek epitedeios (G2006) — needful, fit for the body; “ye give them not those things which are needful to the body”, James 2:16.
Hebrew lavah (H3867) — to lend, here to the LORD; “He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD”, Proverbs 19:17.
usage: “Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry” (Isa 58:7) — the fast God actually chooses.
“be ye warmed and filled” (Jam 2:16) — the words that condemn the speaker.
“lendeth unto the LORD” (Pro 19:17) — who the real creditor is.

pos: n. (the Alsatian Cistercian abbey of 1138, whose abbot joined the Fourth Crusade and whose chaplain wrote its history)
etymology: From a local Alsatian place name of uncertain origin, Latin Parisium.
biblical_def: Pairis in the Vosges above Orbey in Alsace was founded in 1138 from Lucelle. Its historical importance is entirely out of proportion to its size, because its abbot Martin took the cross in 1201, travelled with the Fourth Crusade, and was present when the army turned aside from the Holy Land and sacked Constantinople, a Christian city, in 1204. Martin came home loaded with relics taken from its churches, and his chaplain Gunther of Pairis wrote the Historia Constantinopolitana, which describes the plundering in detail and presents it as pious. This dictionary records Pairis for that book, because it is a rare and valuable thing: a theft narrated by its beneficiaries as devotion. Scripture does not allow the category. The command is unqualified, “Thou shalt not steal” (Exo 20:15), and God says explicitly that he will not take stolen goods as worship, “I hate robbery for burnt offering” (Isa 61:8). Gain taken by violence destroys the taker, “So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain” (Pro 1:19), and the first man in Scripture to take spoil and hide it had the same excuse, “I coveted them, and took them” (Jos 7:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines plunder as goods taken by force; spoil as that which is taken from an enemy; sacrilege as the crime of violating sacred things; a relic as the remains of a saint; and rapine as the act of plundering.
webster_full: PLUNDER, n. That which is taken from an enemy by force; pillage; prey; spoil; also, that which is taken by theft or fraud.
SPOIL, n. That which is taken from others by violence; particularly in war, the plunder taken from an enemy; pillage; booty.
SACRILEGE, n. The crime of violating or profaning sacred things; or the alienating to common purposes what has been appropriated to religious uses.
RELIC, n. That which remains; the remains of the body of a saint, or of any holy person, preserved and venerated.
RAPINE, n. The act of plundering; the seizing and carrying away of things by force; violence; pillage.
scriptures: For I the LORD love judgment, I hate robbery for burnt offering; and I will direct their work in truth, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them.
So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof.

When I saw among the spoils a goodly Babylonish garment, and two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold of fifty shekels weight, then I coveted them, and took them; and, behold, they are hid in the earth in the midst of my tent, and the silver under it.
corruption_summary: Alsatian abbey of 1138: its abbot came home from the sack of Constantinople loaded with stolen relics, and his chaplain wrote it up as piety.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God refuses stolen property offered to him, and says so in words that leave no room for a pious frame, “For I the LORD love judgment, I hate robbery for burnt offering” (Isa 61:8). The eighth commandment has no clause exempting a holy purpose, “Thou shalt not steal” (Exo 20:15). Gunther of Pairis wrote several thousand words of justification and never addressed either sentence.

The second thing is how the self-deception works, because it is not peculiar to crusaders. Achan's confession is remarkable for how ordinary it sounds: he saw, he wanted, he took, and he hid, “I coveted them, and took them; and, behold, they are hid in the earth” (Jos 7:21). Solomon states the end of it as a settled rule, “which taketh away the life of the owners thereof” (Pro 1:19). A relic in a reliquary at Pairis was still somebody else's, taken by force, from fellow Christians.
roots_summary: Hebrew ganab (H1589), to steal; Hebrew gazel (H1498), robbery; Hebrew betsa' (H1215), unjust gain; Hebrew chamad (H2530), to covet; Hebrew taman (H2934), to hide.
roots_lines: Hebrew ganab (H1589) — to steal, without exception; “Thou shalt not steal”, Exodus 20:15.
Hebrew gazel (H1498) — robbery, hated as an offering; “I hate robbery for burnt offering”, Isaiah 61:8.
Hebrew betsa' (H1215) — gain got by violence; “So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain”, Proverbs 1:19.
Hebrew chamad (H2530) — to covet, to desire wrongly; “I coveted them, and took them”, Joshua 7:21.
Hebrew taman (H2934) — to hide, to bury out of sight; “they are hid in the earth”, Joshua 7:21.
usage: “I hate robbery for burnt offering” (Isa 61:8) — the verse the Historia never quotes.
“Thou shalt not steal” (Exo 20:15) — no clause for a holy purpose.
“I coveted them, and took them” (Jos 7:21) — the confession that fits every such case.

pos: n. (the Jura Cistercian abbey of 1123, mother of Salem, Frienisberg, Pairis and Kaisheim)
etymology: French Lucelle, from Latin Lucis Cella, the cell of light, or from Lutzel, little.
biblical_def: Lucelle, Lützel in German, lies in a narrow valley of the Jura exactly on what is now the boundary between France and Switzerland. Founded in 1123 and affiliated to Morimond in 1124, it became one of the most fertile mother houses in the order, sending colonies to Salem, Pairis, Frienisberg, Kaisheim, Bellelay, Neuburg and others, so that much of the Cistercian presence in Alsace, Swabia and the Swiss plateau descends from this one cramped valley. It was suppressed at the French Revolution and almost nothing of the abbey remains above ground. This dictionary records Lucelle for the disproportion between a small place and a long line, and for its Latin name, the cell of light. Scripture is consistent that light is given to be put where it will be seen, “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel” (Mat 5:15), and that the people of God are the ones carrying it, “Ye are the light of the world” (Mat 5:14). The light itself is not ours, “I am the light of the world” (Joh 8:12), and the direction of travel is settled, “the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day” (Pro 4:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines light as that which makes objects visible; a cell as a small close apartment; a candle as a light made of tallow or wax; to kindle as to set on fire; and a colony as a company transplanted from a parent state.
webster_full: LIGHT, n. That ethereal agent or matter which makes objects perceptible to the sense of seeing; also, illumination of mind; instruction; knowledge.
CELL, n. A small or close apartment, as in a prison; also, a small cave or hollow place; the hut of a hermit.
CANDLE, n. A long but small cylindrical body of tallow, wax or spermaceti, containing a wick composed of linen or cotton threads.
KINDLE, v.t. To set on fire; to cause to burn with flame; to light; as, to kindle a fire.
COLONY, n. A company of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country, and remaining subject to the jurisdiction of the parent state.
scriptures: Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house.
Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.
But the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day.
corruption_summary: Jura abbey of 1123, the cell of light: a cramped valley that sent colonies across Alsace, Swabia and Switzerland, and now has almost nothing standing.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one in the name. A cell of light is a contradiction unless the light is meant to leave, and the Lord makes exactly that point about the absurdity of hiding it, “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick” (Mat 5:15). Lucelle's significance lies entirely in what it sent out.

The second thing is the order of the two claims. Christ tells his people they are the light of the world, “Ye are the light of the world” (Mat 5:14), and also says of himself that he is, “I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness” (Joh 8:12). The two are not in competition; one is the source and the other the reflector, and a reflector that forgets which it is goes out. The direction of a genuine light is given plainly, “that shineth more and more unto the perfect day” (Pro 4:18).
roots_summary: Greek luchnos (G3088), a lamp; Greek phos (G5457), light; Greek modios (G3426), a bushel; Hebrew 'or (H216), light; Hebrew nogahh (H5051), brightness.
roots_lines: Greek luchnos (G3088) — a lamp, lit to be set up; “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel”, Matthew 5:15.
Greek phos (G5457) — light, said of his people; “Ye are the light of the world”, Matthew 5:14.
Greek skotia (G4653) — darkness, what the follower escapes; “he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness”, John 8:12.
Hebrew 'orach (H734) — a path, the way of the just; “the path of the just is as the shining light”, Proverbs 4:18.
Hebrew nogahh (H5051) — brightness, increasing to full day; “that shineth more and more unto the perfect day”, Proverbs 4:18.
usage: “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel” (Mat 5:15) — the absurdity the abbey's name risks.
“I am the light of the world” (Joh 8:12) — the source, as against the reflector.
“that shineth more and more unto the perfect day” (Pro 4:18) — the direction of a real light.
